assessment: All 11 retained main-PDF pages were read as text and visually inspected, with five magnifications. Five figures (ten panel/legend records), no standalone tables, one numbered equation plus five reconstructed components, and all 53 printed bibliography entries were inspected. The review adds 38 limited checks, 66 source payback cells and 272 source ordinal ranks corroborated against native vector paths. The general Equation 1 component was tested with synthetic inputs only. All 53 originals and 13 dependencies or scope requirements remain unverified; explicit supplements A/B, licensed inventories and native LCA, conditioning and payback cases are not reproduced. No accepted Paper 1 input was added.

sections.scope: Identity, title, abstract, keywords, dates and licence
sections.assessment: Eight ETH Zurich authors; JCleanProd514(2025)145659, exact DOI retained, CCBY4.0. Received23Dec2024/revised27Mar2025/accepted4May2025/online21May2025. Abstract generalisations require scenario/boundary/payback and allocation qualifications.

Read climate/CCS/CCU/CDR/mineralisation context, European hub/distance/demand, existing cost/LCA findings, static-inventory limitations and objective. Historical projections are not current deployment facts. All supporting original sources remain unverified.
Read LCA workflow/ISO references, prospective inventories, switching and absolute sustainability assessment. No claim of native independent reproduction.

Read conditioned/unconditioned functional units and T versus T+C boundary. Batch full outbound/empty return; pipe one-way. Capture/purification and geological retention outside. Figure1 pressure-loss work allocation must avoid double counting.

Read ISO container, residual heel, carculator_truck, trailer/gross weights/driving cycles, train/barge/HFO and e-fuel ship inventories. Equal fuel efficiency/LHV and future battery assumptions remain conditional.

Read200km and0.3/10Mt/y, LCOT-optimized geometry/inlet pressures/recompression, coatings/trench/scaling, ambient temperatures, and8Mt/y supercritical comparator. These prescribed flows are not pressure-constrained field injection limits.

Read pure1bar30C feed,25bar gas versus70bar>1C sink,16bar liquefaction, AspenPlus assumptions/claimed4% validation, available surface-water cooling and heat/refrigeration inventory models. SI A/B needed for numerical inventories.

Read premise/ecoinvent3.8, REMIND2.1, three SSP2 scenarios and EUR region. Scenarios are conditional pathways, not empirical probabilities; exact software commits and licensed inventories absent locally.

Read Eq1 and definitions, annual hold and linear interpolation. Capital stock and impact/year rates need matched service, timing/horizon, replacements and residual-value conventions. General component reconstructed only with explicit synthetic inputs.
Read15PB categories plus land-use global-impact proxy,7.9% population allocation and70Gtkm/y demand. Geographic and sectoral allocation assumptions need separate disclosure.
Four result subsections and their different boundaries recognized. No mixing T and T+C inventories or same-year snapshots with dynamic cohorts.

Read4g/tkm example,40x truck comparison, construction burdens, projected reductions/rankings and three fuel-system trends. HFO mix intentionally remains static; blanket72-93% reduction wording overreaches it. Batteries/e-fuels uncertain, costs and access can alter choice.

Read25bar-sink distance crossovers125/340km in2040, dense70bar sink and batch liquefaction comparison. Missing SI means native crossover curves and component energy duties are not independently reconstructed.

Read Figure3 eight switching years,66 Figure4 selected switches,49finite17X, grouped exceptions, lifetime caveat and pipeline replacement. Broad under3/fossil-to-pipe wording is qualified by native cases up to38years.

Read EF3.0/16-category ranks, onshore/offshore differences, electric-truck and ship tradeoffs, GVA allocation and all impact ranges/claimed absolute sustainability. Figure5 explicitly has two offshore categories where HFO ranks above dense pipelines.

Read climate/conditioning/access/payback and future pathways conclusions. Main body14/16 offshore minimum differs from all-category conclusion. Upper-bound.075% alone does not establish fit within entire.023-.074% sector allocation range.
Read eight author contribution statements including JN software/validation and PO software/methodology. Authorship declaration is provenance, not independent validation.
Read disclosed ChatGPT use for readability/language and authors taking responsibility. Does not establish the substance correct or incorrect.
Read AB industry review committees/ownership declarations and other-author statements. Retained as provenance; no unsupported inference of misconduct.
Read DemoUpCARMA Swiss Federal Office funding and Horizon2020ACCSESS grant101022487. Not a current operational or data-availability guarantee.

sections.scope: Appendix A Supplementary data and Data availability
sections.assessment: Read explicit online SI at article DOI, models stated to be included in SI, data licensed from ecoinvent. Neither SI/code nor licence/assets verified locally; local absence is not online absence.
53 native entries text-read/rendered and geometry preserved in bibliography JSON. Their originals and further literature chains are unverified; zero new primary-source edges claimed.

visuals.object: Figure 1a: batch boundary, arrows and caption
visuals.inspection: Read capture, conditioning, full/empty ISO paths, container/vehicle/infrastructure/fuel inputs, sink conditioning and use/storage. Red T versus purple T+C; blue CO₂ and green tank arrows. Capture/storage operations are outside; returning heel is not an implied vent loss.

visuals.object: Figure 1b: pipeline boundary and shared legend
visuals.inspection: Read the split between preparation to outlet pressure and loss-related work to inlet pressure, construction, recompression and sink conditioning. Loss work belongs to T, with other conditioning added in T+C. No flow or utility magnitudes appear in this schematic.

Read all ten modes, colours, markers, years, gCO₂e/tkm axis and dotted initial segments. SSP2-NDC, T only, all lifecycle phases in the same year. The small gas line is not uniformly below batch modes. Curves are not substituted for native use-phase arrays.

visuals.object: Figure 2 offshore panel and shared caption
visuals.inspection: Read seven modes, the approximately flat HFO line, e-fuel declines and dense/gas capacities. The same T, SSP2-NDC and snapshot convention applies. The missing prospective HFO market explains its fixed baseline; no pressure or density correction is inferred.

visuals.object: Figure 3 cumulative-payback plot, labels and caption
visuals.inspection: Read train use-only baseline, eight dense 0.3 Mt/y switches, 40-year lifetime and labels 3.3/5.7/7.1/6.7/6.4/6.7/7.3/8.1 years. Cumulative normalized units need an annual-service interpretation. The sequence is nonmonotonic and 2040 exceeds three years.

visuals.object: Figure 4a: all 45 onshore cells and group outlines
visuals.inspection: Inspected at 3× with every row/column label, X, dash, zero and (16). Saved 34 finite and 11 X entries; the H₂-to-electric-truck case exceeds lifetime. A/C/D are the authors’ group labels; 45 reverse directions are absent.

visuals.object: Figure 4b: all 21 offshore cells and shared caption
visuals.inspection: Inspected at 3×: 15 finite and 6 X entries. HFO-to-gas is 20/12 years and e-fuel-to-dense is 14–31. The total is 49 finite of 66 selected directions. A displayed zero is not proof of instantaneous payoff.

At 3×, traced all 160 ordinal ranks and corroborated the transcription with native vector paths. Dense 10 Mt/y ranks first in 16 categories; electric trucks rank worse than H₂ in 11 and diesel in 4. Rank gaps are not cardinal benefits.

At 3×, traced all 112 ordinal ranks and corroborated native vector paths. Dense 10 Mt/y ranks first in 14 categories; HFO is first for water use and freshwater eutrophication. These exceptions conflict with page 10’s broad conclusion. Bubble magnitudes remain undigitized.

visuals.object: Figure 5 category labels, circle-area legend and caption
visuals.inspection: Read all sixteen labels in native order. SSP2-NDC, T, 2070, all lifecycle phases in the same year. Circle area keys are 0.1%, 1% and 4.5% of European carrying capacity. Land use uses current global impact, not a defined PB; no aggregate sustainability score is inferred.

equations.printed: Native Eq(1): integral Iop,old dt = Iinv,new(ts) + integral Iop,new dt, ts to ts+Delta_tcpb
equations.check: Definitions read at magnification: ts switching year; Iinv climate impact stock; Iop impact rate/year for consistent integration. Source states annual constant values and linearly interpolated year values. No native LCA arrays supplied.

equations.printed: Independent annual-hold first-crossing derivation: sum prior annual savings + fractional-year saving = new capital
equations.check: Implemented first_payback: for positive current saving s, tau=j+(capital-Sprior)/s if that year reaches equality. None is no crossing within supplied horizon. Changes in utilization, replacements and later reversal require explicit treatment; no native cases reproduced.

equations.printed: Independent constant-rate limit: Delta_tcpb=Iinv/(Iop,old-Iop,new) for positive saving
equations.check: Checked fractional crossing and scale invariance against analytical limit. Nonpositive saving has no positive-capital payoff within constant scenario. Synthetic values only; equality alone does not guarantee permanent superiority with varying rates.

equations.printed: Independent reference-flow conversion: gCO2e/tkm * distance_km /1000 = kgCO2e/t transported
equations.check: Selected4g/tkm at100km=.4kg/t;0.7Gt/y=>.28MtCO2e/y. Transport-only conditional conversion, not avoided/permanent CO2 or an all-pipeline factor.

equations.printed: Independent demand and allocation:0.7Gt/y*100km=70Gtkm/y; sector percent=(70/1800)*GVA percent
equations.check: Reconstructs.023333-.073889% sector range; population allocation Europe7.9% is a separate stage. Upper bound<.075% cannot alone guarantee compatibility with lower or even strict upper rounded GVA threshold. Land use uses different proxy denominator.

equations.printed: Independent container conservation: full=tare+fill; return=tare+.04fill; delivered=.96fill
equations.check: Conditional20.7t initial fill gives29.9tfull,.828theel,10.028treturn,19.872tdelivery. Does not independently verify native allocation or claim4% atmospheric loss.

variables.name: Functional unit and reference mass
variables.assumption: T and T+C use different inlet states. Preserve the printed ton/t definitions and native inventory denominator; captured, delivered, injected, avoided and permanently retained mass are distinct.

variables.name: ISO tare and capacity
variables.assumption: Manufacturer case at 16 bar; capacity is treated conditionally as initial fill only for the mass diagnostic.

variables.name: Residual heel and return
variables.assumption: Gas remains at maximum allowable pressure and returns; no vent-loss inference. Native freight normalization remains unverified.

variables.name: Gross truck, trailer and early battery mass
variables.assumption: Truck, driver and freight. The 2020/2025 battery cases explicitly exceed this mass; applicable road limits and actual weights are not verified.

variables.name: Driving cycle and range
variables.assumption: carculator uses target speed and gross mass; autonomy is not actual case distance or a fleet schedule.

variables.name: Fuels, propulsion and exhaust
variables.unit: diesel, electricity, H₂, HFO, methanol and ammonia
variables.assumption: Production pathways, equal shipping efficiency, LHV and pollutant inventories are case-dependent; missing quantities are not filled.

variables.name: Transport state
variables.unit: 16 bar liquid; 15–30 bar gas; 80–350 bar dense
variables.assumption: Pressure datum is not explicit. Batch temperature is slightly below boiling, with no exact temperature invented; ambient pipelines use 15°C onshore and 4°C offshore.

variables.name: Pipeline length, flow, comparator and lifetime
variables.unit: 200 km; 0.3/10 Mt/y; 8 Mt/y comparator; 40 y in Figure 3
variables.assumption: Prescribed transport design and lifetime, rather than annual safe sink service, actual utilization or universal asset life.

variables.name: Optimized design variables
variables.unit: diameters, inlet pressure, station count and electricity
variables.assumption: The LCOT model has modified work allocation. Exact parameters and native code remain missing; a cost optimum need not minimize environmental impacts.

variables.name: Geometry, coating, burial and scaling
variables.unit: steel, coating, trench and cross-section quantities
variables.assumption: Some natural-gas pipeline analogues are scaled; no actual dimensions, failure properties or field calibration are inferred.

variables.name: Conditioning feed
variables.assumption: Capture and purification are upstream; no mixture assumption, datum conversion or upstream heat credit is inferred.

variables.name: Sink receiving states
variables.unit: 25 bar gas or 70 bar dense above 1°C
variables.assumption: Historical terminal conditions do not establish bottom-hole limits, injectivity or retained-carbon guarantees.

variables.name: Conditioning duties and validation
variables.unit: compression, pumping, cooling, refrigeration and heating; claimed ±4%
variables.assumption: Aspen v11.1, Deng assumptions, surface water and ecoinvent models; the complete numerical case and supplier inventory requires unverified supplements.

variables.name: Background and geography
variables.assumption: EUR covers the EU and UK. Exact commits and licensed assets are absent locally; Asian use requires a disclosed proxy.

variables.name: Scenario and time
variables.assumption: Common SSP2 narrative, without empirical probabilities. Five-year then ten-year plot steps are interpolated annually; snapshots are not dynamic cohorts.

variables.name: Switching time and payback
variables.assumption: The first cumulative crossing needs explicit service scale, horizon, lifetime, renewal, residual-value and reversal conventions.

variables.name: New construction impact
variables.unit: impact stock, e.g. gCO₂e at a normalized service scale
variables.assumption: Capital enters once at switching; it cannot be added to annual rates without consistent stock/time accounting.

variables.name: Old and new use-phase impacts
variables.unit: impact/year at the same service scale
variables.assumption: Equation 1 integrates annual rates. Annual-hold discretization differs from a continuously varying-rate integral.

variables.name: Intensities and lifecycle snapshots
variables.assumption: Figures 2/5 place lifecycle phases in the same year. The 4 g value is a selected pipeline example; 38/43/85 g are construction-only truck figures for 2020.

variables.name: Global and European category allocation
variables.assumption: Population Europe excluding Russia differs from EUR/EU-27 scope; allocation is not physical reservoir safety.

variables.name: Network demand and freight GVA
variables.assumption: Equal GVA per tkm yields 0.023333–0.073889% sector allocation; routing and annual injection are not reproduced.

variables.name: Absolute shares and ranks
variables.unit: percent of European carrying capacity; ranks 1–10 or 1–7
variables.assumption: Circle area represents share; ranks are ordinal. Ranges do not provide whole-chain avoided-emission factors or cardinal benefits.

variables.name: Payback labels and symbols
variables.assumption: Figure 3 decimals differ from Figure 4 integers. No rounding rule is supplied; zero is not instantaneous, (16) exceeds lifetime and dashes are unassessed directions.

variables.name: LCIA versions and missing absolute arrays
variables.assumption: Exact characterization, normalization and PB versions require clarification. Land use is a global-impact substitute, rather than a defined PB threshold.

claims.claim: Paris 1.5°C and net-zero goals require major reductions and removals.
claims.assessment: Historical scientific and policy context; the cited originals remain unverified.

claims.claim: CCS can support hard-to-abate cement, steel and chemical industries.
claims.assessment: Background role, rather than a performance or counterfactual inventory of this transport model.

claims.claim: Permanent storage of DAC or biogenic CO₂ can enable removal.
claims.assessment: Conditional on the complete lifecycle and storage; this transport boundary does not demonstrate removal.

claims.claim: CCU can help replace fossil feedstocks in chemical production.
claims.assessment: Background; utilization does not automatically provide permanent storage.

claims.claim: CO₂ may enter long-lived mineralised construction products.
claims.assessment: Carbon fate and substitution must be established for each case.

claims.claim: European capture deployment may reach the gigatonne scale by mid-century.
claims.assessment: IEA 2020 projection, rather than current operating capacity or pressure-constrained storage service.

claims.claim: Northern Lights, Porthos and Coda are pioneering storage-hub examples.
claims.assessment: Historical cited plans and receiving conditions; current operation was not checked.

claims.claim: Pioneering chains can span several thousand kilometres.
claims.assessment: Cited geographical and cost context; no native chain mass or service inventory is supplied here.

claims.claim: About one-third of European emitters are over 100 km from potential storage.
claims.assessment: Cited IEA 2020 statistic; the exact dataset and point-source weighting remain unverified.

claims.claim: Pipelines are often least-cost for large onshore flows, while fossil-fuel ships can compete at long offshore distances.
claims.assessment: Cost context depends on the original case; it does not establish an environmental optimum or project feasibility.

claims.claim: Transport selection requires several criteria beyond cost.
claims.assessment: Methodological motivation, rather than a validated weighted decision rule.

claims.claim: Existing CCS LCAs frequently assume pipelines and static or historical inventories.
claims.assessment: The four review originals and their literature coverage have not been independently verified.

claims.claim: Pipeline networks can require years or decades and multinational agreements.
claims.assessment: Context references do not supply exact local construction or permission durations.

claims.claim: Batch modes are needed in pioneering, small or remote chains.
claims.assessment: Context and access assumptions; no implication that every batch mode is available everywhere.

claims.claim: Burger 2024 reports transport dominating more than half of impact categories and reaching 152 kgCO₂e/t transported for a Swiss–North Sea chain.
claims.assessment: Quote from a different original, not a B2-13 per-tkm factor or whole-chain avoidance value; original DOI 104039 is not retained locally.

claims.claim: Projected capture expansion in 2035–2070 overlaps the European energy transition.
claims.assessment: Historical IEA and strategy projections, rather than current forecasts independently validated by this audit.

claims.claim: premise couples IAM changes with LCA; several futures address projection uncertainty.
claims.assessment: Conditional scenario modelling; no empirical scenario probabilities are established.

claims.claim: The study follows ISO LCA methodology and assesses transport through 2100.
claims.assessment: Authors’ methods statement; native cases, inventories and standards compliance were not independently reproduced.

claims.claim: Boundary T uses 1 t of conditioned CO₂ over 1 km, excluding conditioning; batch transport includes full outbound and empty return trips, and pipelines are one-way.
claims.assessment: Figure 1 confirms the boundary; equal service and freight normalization require native code. Returning heel is not an atmospheric loss.

claims.claim: Boundary T+C uses 1 t of unconditioned CO₂ over 1 km and includes transport and storage conditioning.
claims.assessment: Pure feed at 1 bar and 30°C is assumed; capture, purification and geological injection or retention remain outside the inventory.

claims.claim: Pipeline work to overcome pressure loss belongs to T; other initial and final conditioning belongs to T+C.
claims.assessment: The Figure 1 split must avoid double counting; the modified native algorithm remains unavailable locally.

claims.claim: Batch CO₂ is liquid at 16 bar slightly below boiling; gas pipelines use 15–30 bar and dense pipelines 80–350 bar at ambient temperature.
claims.assessment: The main PDF does not give pressure datum or exact batch temperature; no conversion or state correction was invented.

claims.claim: The ISO tank has a 9.2 t tare and 20.7 t CO₂ capacity at 16 bar.
claims.assessment: Conditional mass arithmetic was checked; the manufacturer original remains unverified.

claims.claim: Four percent of the CO₂ remains as gas for the return trip at maximum allowable pressure.
claims.assessment: A conservative heel assumption, rather than vented loss; native LCI normalization has not been verified.

claims.claim: carculator_truck supplies diesel, battery-electric and fuel-cell truck inventories.
claims.assessment: The stated model uses per-second target speed and gross mass; its exact version, data and outputs are not retained.

claims.claim: Loaded truck gross mass is about 44 t; battery trucks exceed that mass in 2020 and 2025 and fall below it after 2025.
claims.assessment: Explicit feasibility caveat for early electric cases; actual weights and applicable national road limits remain unverified.

claims.claim: The baseline regional cycle has 400 km autonomy, with 150 km urban and 800 km long-haul sensitivities.
claims.assessment: Autonomy is not the route length or fleet schedule; sensitivity curves are referred to the unverified supplement.

claims.claim: Electric trains, diesel barges and HFO container ships use ecoinvent cutoff 3.8 inventories.
claims.assessment: Licensed inventories are not retained or verified; supplier, version and geography matter.

claims.claim: Methanol ship fuel uses DAC CO₂, heat pumps and electrolytic H₂.
claims.assessment: Foreground lineage is attributed to Hank and premise; no complete feed, utility or supplier balance appears in the main PDF.

claims.claim: Ammonia uses Haber–Bosch synthesis, electrolytic H₂ and nitrogen from air separation.
claims.assessment: Mayer and premise provide the stated lineage; the main PDF does not give a complete utility inventory.

claims.claim: Alternative-fuel ships use HFO tank-to-wheel efficiency with fuel demand scaled by LHV; exhaust inventories come from IMO and Schwarzkopf.
claims.assessment: Equal efficiency is an assumption, rather than an independent engine model; pollutant pathways and original cases remain open.

claims.claim: The 200 km pipelines at 0.3 and 10 Mt/y are optimized for lowest levelized transport cost.
claims.assessment: These are prescribed transport flows, not field injectivity limits; minimum cost need not minimize LCIA impacts.

claims.claim: Gas outlet pressure is 15 bar and dense outlet pressure 80 bar; inlet pressures and recompression stations vary.
claims.assessment: The conditioning split is documented, but native pressure-work arrays and optimization cases were not reproduced.

claims.claim: Steel and coating follow geometry, burial follows trench recommendations, and some inventories scale with cross-section; pipelines use ambient 15°C onshore and 4°C offshore without insulation.
claims.assessment: Analogue and scaling assumptions need the actual dimensions, inventories and native supplement.

claims.claim: An 8 Mt/y supercritical comparator has lower density and viscosity than dense CO₂.
claims.assessment: Specific thermodynamic states and the legacy inventory are needed; no universal property ranking is inferred.

claims.claim: Gas at 25 bar represents Coda and Porthos receiving or injection conditions.
claims.assessment: Historical source conditions do not establish a bottom-hole operating limit or deliverability case.

claims.claim: Dense CO₂ at 70 bar and above 1°C represents the Northern Lights Phase 1 pipeline inlet.
claims.assessment: Historical receiving state, rather than a fracture threshold or annual storage-service guarantee.

claims.claim: The 16 bar liquefaction model follows Deng; other processes use AspenPlus and are said to reproduce liquefaction energy within ±4%.
claims.assessment: This is the authors’ validation claim. Exact states, errors, original data and native cases remain unverified; no complete numerical balance is provided in the main PDF.

claims.claim: Compression, pumping, cooling, refrigeration and heating are considered, with surface-water cooling and ecoinvent equipment models; flowsheets and inventories are in supplements.
claims.assessment: Naming operations does not close a capture-to-ship inventory. Missing duties are not set to zero.

claims.claim: premise modifies ecoinvent 3.8 for IAM energy, industry and fuel changes.
claims.assessment: Conditional background construction; no licensed inventory or version-matched native model was rerun.

claims.claim: The three SSP2 scenarios are NDC, Base and PkBudg500, the last with a global 500 Gt CO₂ budget through 2100.
claims.assessment: Cited scenario semantics were read; probabilities and the underlying IAM implementation were not independently audited.

claims.claim: Results use 5-year steps in 2020–2050 and 10-year steps through 2100; REMIND has 12 regions, with EUR covering the EU and UK.
claims.assessment: Twelve plotted time points were checked. European averages vary by country and require explicit proxy disclosure for Asian applications.

claims.claim: Carbon payback equates cumulative old operating impacts with new capital plus cumulative new operating impacts.
claims.assessment: The dimensional and first-crossing component was reconstructed with synthetic inputs; the conceptual payback reference remains unverified.

claims.claim: Equation 1 is discretized with annual constant impacts, using linear interpolation to obtain each year’s values.
claims.assessment: Annual-hold integration passes constant-rate and fractional-year checks; the native annual arrays are missing.

claims.claim: The assessment uses 15 EF-based planetary boundaries and substitutes current global impact for land use.
claims.assessment: There are not 16 defined planetary-boundary thresholds. Exact EF 3.0/3.1 factor alignment needs the supplement and original sources.

claims.claim: Europe receives 7.9% of global safe operating space by population, excluding Russia.
claims.assessment: An equality-allocation choice; population data and alignment with the EUR and EU-27 geographical scopes remain unverified.

claims.claim: A 0.7 Gt/y capture projection and 100 km mean proximity yield 70 Gtkm/y.
claims.assessment: The product was checked; it does not reproduce routing or pressure-constrained annual injection.

claims.claim: Pipeline climate impacts can already be as low as 4 gCO₂e/tkm because of low operating burdens and high lifetime throughput.
claims.assessment: A selected large-pipeline example, rather than a factor for every capacity, state or complete chain; the exact inventory remains missing.

claims.claim: Trucks can exceed 40 times pipeline climate impact; 2020 construction burdens are 38, 43 and 85 gCO₂e/tkm for diesel, H₂ and electric trucks.
claims.assessment: Those three values cover construction, rather than total truck impacts; gross-to-cargo ratio and return assumptions qualify the comparison.

claims.claim: By 2100 climate impacts are said to decline 72–93%, with 127 g/tkm average truck reduction and 86% pipeline versus 81% truck reductions.
claims.assessment: The HFO mix is held constant and its Figure 2 curve is flat, so broad all-mode wording overreaches it. Native averages and percentages were not independently reproduced.

claims.claim: Non-pipeline climate rankings change until 2030 and then stabilize across scenarios.
claims.assessment: Conditional native projection; the other scenario curves are in unverified supplementary material, rather than a proof across all plausible futures.

claims.claim: Electric and e-fuel impacts fall strongly in 2020–2035 with electricity decarbonization, then with changes in steel, cement and fuels.
claims.assessment: A model dependency, rather than independent measurement; native scenario arrays are needed.

claims.claim: Diesel-like fuel impacts decline with biofuel and e-fuel blending, except in the pessimistic Base case.
claims.assessment: Fuel-market assumption, rather than a guarantee of improved diesel-engine efficiency; native inventories remain open.

claims.claim: HFO ship impacts remain constant because premise lacks a prospective HFO market mix.
claims.assessment: Explicitly asymmetric background treatment; qualifies comparisons across fuels and broad reduction or robustness claims.

claims.claim: Pipeline maturity gives the authors confidence in inventories, while trains and e-fuel ships are alternatives with larger uncertainties.
claims.assessment: Confidence and cost literature do not independently validate field performance or define a weighted environmental score.

claims.claim: Electric and H₂ trucks are expected to beat diesel climate impacts across autonomy assumptions, with substantial battery supply-chain uncertainty.
claims.assessment: Conditional supplementary result; retain early gross-mass limits and variation in country of production and raw materials.

claims.claim: Barges may be cheaper than trains above 500 km, while trucks can suit shorter distances or restricted access.
claims.assessment: An economic case threshold, rather than an environmental or universally applicable one; the exact original costs remain unverified.

claims.claim: For a 25 bar gas sink in 2040, dense versus gas pipeline crossovers are 125 km at 0.3 Mt/y and 340 km at 10 Mt/y.
claims.assessment: Supplement-based source quotes, rather than independently reproduced curves, universal route choices or reservoir pressure limits.

claims.claim: For a 70 bar dense sink, dense pipelines have the lowest climate impact regardless of transport distance.
claims.assessment: Within the modeled cases, backgrounds and sink conditions; native conditioning arrays remain unverified.

claims.claim: Batch liquefaction has greater conditioning climate impact than pipeline preparation.
claims.assessment: Boundary-specific supplementary claim; it does not supply capture utilities or a matched-source heat credit.

claims.claim: Train-to-0.3 Mt/y dense-pipeline payback ranges from 3.3 years for a 2020 switch to 8.1 years in 2080.
claims.assessment: All eight labels were read: 2040 is 6.7 years, and the sequence decreases in 2040 and 2050. It is not universally under three years.

claims.claim: For 2040, 49 of 66 switches benefit within less than six months to 38 years, while 17 increase cumulative impacts.
claims.assessment: Counts were corroborated from every cell. These are 66 selected directions, rather than all 132 directed pairs; the finite count includes a payback beyond lifetime.

claims.claim: Batch-to-pipeline switches usually pay back within seven years, and often within three for dense pipelines, subject to exceptions.
claims.assessment: Retain train-to-small-dense at 6.7 years, e-fuel ships at 14–31 years and electric-truck cases at 30 or 6 years, rather than adopting an unqualified headline rule.

claims.claim: Switching diesel or HFO transport to pipelines is said to give benefits within three years.
claims.assessment: Overbroad versus Figure 4: HFO to 0.3 or 10 Mt/y gas pipelines is 20 or 12 years. Preserve mode, capacity, year and boundary instead of guessing corrected values.

claims.claim: Switching between pipelines rarely benefits unless capacity increases substantially or a more efficient dense line is introduced.
claims.assessment: Native X and 3–38 year cases remain conditional on horizon, lifetime and replacement conventions. Similar intensities alone do not establish payback.

claims.claim: EF 3.0 rankings put dense pipelines first in all 16 onshore categories and 14 of 16 offshore categories.
claims.assessment: All 272 discrete ranks were corroborated against native vector paths. Offshore exceptions are water use and freshwater eutrophication; absolute magnitudes and factor versions remain open.

claims.claim: After dense pipelines, gas pipelines outperform batch modes onshore, but only some categories offshore.
claims.assessment: Figure 5 is an ordinal comparison for 2070, T and SSP2-NDC; it does not define a weighted aggregate winner.

claims.claim: Electric trucks rank worse than H₂ trucks in 11 of 16 categories and diesel trucks in 4, largely due to battery burdens.
claims.assessment: Counts reconstruct from the native ordinals; the mechanism needs licensed LCI. Rank separation does not measure impact magnitude.

claims.claim: HFO ships have greater climate impact but perform better in about half of the other categories than alternative-fuel ships.
claims.assessment: The ordinal replay gives 9 of 15 against ammonia and 7 of 15 against methanol. This does not define an aggregate weighted winner.

claims.claim: EU-27 road freight of 1,800 Gtkm and 0.6–1.9% GVA imply a 0.023–0.074% sector allocation for 70 Gtkm.
claims.assessment: Arithmetic gives 0.023333–0.073889%. It assumes linear GVA per tkm; future CO₂-sector contribution and geographical alignment were not measured.

claims.claim: Overall shares span 0.000003–4.8% onshore and 0.000005–0.46% offshore.
claims.assessment: Quoted ranges across categories and modes, rather than independent absolute-LCI reproduction. Bubble areas were not converted to exact impacts.

claims.claim: Dense pipeline impacts are below 0.075%, with ecotoxicity, minerals and particulates at 0.012–0.075% and other categories below 0.023%.
claims.assessment: This upper bound does not establish that every case fits the entire GVA allocation range; exact category impacts are missing. Actual exceedance is not established either.

claims.claim: Onshore batch impacts reach 0.4–4.8% in critical categories; diesel trucks or barges can exceed 0.075% in up to ten categories and other land modes in up to seven.
claims.assessment: Scenario and category statements need native absolute arrays. Land use uses a proxy denominator, so these are not sixteen common physical PB thresholds.

claims.claim: Most offshore category-mode impacts are below 0.075%, suggesting environmentally preferable offshore transport.
claims.assessment: Equivalent routes, service and sinks must be compared; different onshore and offshore networks are not automatically interchangeable.

supplements: Page 4 explicitly refers to Supplementary Material A for flowsheets, the pipeline model and work allocation, and B for transport and conditioning inventories and impacts. Pages 5–7 refer to Figures A.9–A.13. Page 10 links the article DOI and states that models are included in supplementary material and data can be licensed from ecoinvent. Neither supplement, native model files, inventories nor license entitlement was verified locally; the PDF has no embedded files. External retrieval remains paused under the user’s Chrome instruction. reproduction: audit_prospective_transport.py reconstructs the general Equation 1 annual-hold first-crossing component using explicitly synthetic equal-service inputs. Analytical, fractional-year, scaling, horizon and reversal tests pass. It produces 38 limited mass/unit/allocation/count/rank checks, 66 manually transcribed Figure 4 cells, 272 Figure 5 ordinal ranks corroborated by PDF vector geometry and 40 analyst annual rows. It does not reproduce the authors’ actual payback cases, absolute LCIA, licensed ecoinvent/premise/carculator models, Aspen conditioning or cost-optimized pipelines. Missing native inventories remain null. Bubble areas were not converted into exact impacts.
paper1_use: Recognize prior prospective transport LCA and construction-versus-operating carbon-payback work. Preserve T/T+C boundaries, full/empty heel routing, region, scenario, lifetime, allocation and category tradeoffs. Retain train/HFO/e-fuel payback exceptions, the offshore 14/16 ranking, static HFO background and conditional planetary budget. This paper does not close matched capture-to-ship utilities, pressure-constrained annual reservoir service or retained/avoided-carbon factors. The existing combined 1.5 MPa HOLD remains; no accepted operating/GHG inputs or current numerical results changed.
